Two weeks after initial improvement, she developed intermittent night sweats, fevers up to 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), fatigue, and weight loss of 10 kg (22.05 lb). At presentation, her temperature was 37.8 °C (100 °F); heart rate, 71 beats/min; and blood pressure, 126/80 mm Hg. Findings of chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans were normal. An initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min and first-degree atrioventricular block. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TEE) revealed a normally functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve without vegetations. A TEE (Figure 1) showed normal valvular function and a thickened aortic root. case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

     message imposes on YOU.

       the case?"

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {

    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 72-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic aortic valve implanted 6 years prior to presentation was evaluated for fevers, malaise, and weight loss. Five months prior, she developed fevers and chills while visiting the island of Elba, where she consumed raw milk products. Two weeks after initial improvement, she developed intermittent night sweats, fevers up to 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), fatigue, and weight loss of 10 kg (22.05 lb). At presentation, her temperature was 37.8 °C (100 °F); heart rate, 71 beats/min; and blood pressure, 126/80 mm Hg. Physical examination was normal except for a grade 2 cardiac systolic ejection murmur. Laboratory findings revealed a normal complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and transaminase level. C-reactive protein level was 13 mg/L (reference, <5 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 50 mm/h (reference, <20 mm/h). Rheumatoid factor level was 68 U/mL (reference, <14 U/mL). Results ofTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination and HIV testing were negative. Two sets of blood cultures showed no growth after 7 days. Findings of chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans were normal. An initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min and first-degree atrioventricular block. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TEE) revealed a normally functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve without vegetations. A TEE (Figure 1) showed normal valvular function and a thickened aortic root. Results of serologic testing forBrucellaspp andBartonella henselaewere negative. Phase I and II IgG titers forCoxiella burnetiiwere ≥1:10 240 (reference, <1:40). Phase I IgM titer was 1:160 and phase II IgM titer was 1:320 (reference, <1:40).

case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2
